clean_story:
Cold air rushing downhill. Gravity-driven gusts.

The name katabatic comes from the Greek katabatikos, meaning "going downhill," describing how dense, cold air flows downward like water over a slope. Most see wind as chaotic, but katabatic winds are disciplined: they form when air cools over high, flat terrain—like Antarctica’s ice sheets or Greenland’s glaciers—and grows heavier than the warmer air below. This cold pool spills downhill, accelerating with gravity, funneling through valleys at speeds up to 200 miles per hour in places like Adélie Land. In California’s Central Valley, these winds dry orchards overnight, preventing frost damage. In Alaska, they clear fog from airport runways by sheer force. No other wind is so predictable in its descent, so relentless in its path.

Three related subjects are mountain breezes, foehn winds and atmospheric rivers.
